turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come in, Lachlan. Sorry about the wait, the clinic's been flat out. How've you been travelling?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Not great. I'm wheezy, and my chest feels tight.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay. Tell me how that's been for you, whatever comes to mind.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. I just can't get a proper breath, like I'm breathing through a straw.
[SEG0005] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He picked up a cold over the weekend, sniffly and a bit off, and then the wheeze started.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): Lachlan, when did the wheeze actually kick off, do you reckon?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): The footy was on and I couldn't even yell at the telly. Sounded like a squeaky door, Mum said.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sounds rough. I'm still after the timing though — days, or longer than that?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Maybe Thursday. Could've been Friday. I lose track.
[SEG0010] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Thursday night, I'm pretty sure. He got home from school crook, and Friday morning he was puffing on the lounge.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Any fever? Felt hot or shivery at all?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Nah. Not hot. Just the cough, and that tight feeling.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is the cough bringing anything up?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Bit of gunk in the mornings. Clear, sort of. Not green.
[SEG0015] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And he's been up at night with it. Two nights, maybe three. Last night it was about two.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain in there?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. It aches when I cough. Not a sharp pain, just sore after.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): From what I'm hearing, I'd leave steroid tablets out of it. Usual puffers, and I'll see you next week if it's just the tail of that cold.
[SEG0019] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Can I just say what he's been doing with the puffers first? I don't think that plan quite fits.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Of course, go on. What puffers has he got, Lachlan?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, the blue one. Or — wait, the brown? I always mix those up. One of them tastes worse.

[SEG0022] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He really does mix them. Blue is Ventolin, the reliever. Brown is Qvar, the preventer. He's meant to take the brown one twice a day, but I don't think he's touched it since the cold started.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Easy mix-up. Lachlan, the blue Ventolin — how many times a day have you been using it?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Maybe five, six times a day. Well, actually, more like that when I'm walking to the bus — that sets the wheeze off.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): And each go, how many puffs?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Two. I think. The chemist said two.
[SEG0027] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Yes, two puffs. It's the hundred microgram Ventolin. And the Qvar is fifty micrograms, two puffs morning and night, when he remembers.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else from the chemist? Tablets?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Panadol, sometimes, for a headache. Not every day.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is the headache still there?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Mostly gone. I had one Sunday, that's all.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines that you know of?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. I don't think so.
[SEG0034] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Nothing. No drug allergies on his list, and he's never had a reaction I've seen.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long have you had asthma?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Since I was little. Year two, maybe. I don't know exactly.
[SEG0037] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Since he was about seven. He's seventeen now. Never been in hospital for it, no intensive care, nothing like that.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, or vape?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Never. If my mate's smoking near me it sets my chest off, though.
[SEG0040] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He lives with his mum and his little brother. I'm Priya, his support worker — I do appointments and a couple of arvos a week. He doesn't drink.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thanks, Priya. Anyone else in the family with asthma?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): My brother had it. He grew out of it, I think. Mum doesn't have it.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, I'll have a listen. Big breath in for me... and out. Once more.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): There's a wheeze on both sides, a bit louder on the right. No crackles. You're talking in full sentences, and you're not pulling in at the neck, which is reassuring.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): The nurse did your peak flow before you came through. She read 320 litres a minute. The card says your best is five hundred and ten, so you're down around sixty percent.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Is 320 bad?
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Lower than I want after a virus, yeah. Not a collapse, but not something to shrug off.

[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): That frequency, and a peak flow of 320, changes my mind. Forget next week and no tablets. We'll add prednisolone, forty milligrams by mouth, once every morning for five days, with breakfast.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Tablets? I don't know, doctor. I hate swallowing them.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): I get that. It's only five mornings, with food so your stomach doesn't play up, and it should pull the wheeze down quicker than the puffers on their own.

[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Blue Ventolin stays the one you grab when you're tight, two puffs. If you need it more than every four hours, or you can't finish a sentence, you go to emergency. Don't sit on it.
[SEG0052] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll stick the prednisolone on the fridge and I'll actually hand him the brown one. Two puffs, morning and night, even when he feels fine.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Please do. Lachlan — blue is for the wheeze, when you need it. Brown is the every-day one. You've mixed them up, heaps of people do.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Blue when I'm wheezy. Brown every day. I'll try.
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): I reckon this is a flare of your asthma after that cold. Not an infection that needs antibiotics — sputum's clear, no fever — so no antibiotic from me.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): So I can go to school tomorrow?
[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you're breathing easier at breakfast, yes, but no sport this week. If you're still huffing in the morning, stay home and ring the clinic.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me on Friday, or sooner if you're worse. Reception'll book it on the way out. We'll see how the five days are treating you.

doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.

bad.reason: Wheeze current; walking to bus triggers it. Onset Thursday night came from caregiver, not patient; patient was uncertain.

bad.text: Qvar (generic_name=beclomethasone, dose=50 microgram, 2 puffs, frequency=morning and night, indication=asthma preventer, status=discontinued, reported_by=caregiver)

omissions.text: Cold symptoms preceded the asthma flare: he was sniffly/a bit off over the weekend and got home from school feeling crook before the wheeze started.
Shortness of breath was specifically described as not being able to get a proper breath / 'breathing through a straw'.
No shivery feelings/rigors were reported along with no fever.
Ventolin use was more than 5–6 times/day when walking to the bus triggered wheeze; the recorded frequency understates this.
Qvar was prescribed as a preventer 'when he remembers'; the recorded status 'discontinued' is wrong—he is meant to take it regularly but has likely been non-adherent since the cold started.
Prednisolone was specifically to be taken with breakfast.
Peak flow of 320 L/min was interpreted as about 60% of his personal best.

The clinician initially said they would leave steroid tablets out and review next week, but the caregiver disagreed that this plan fit because of how he had been using his puffers, prompting revision of the plan.
Reception was to book the Friday follow-up on the way out.
